summary:
Kaduna is a state in northern Nigeria and stands under the national framework; its own criminal law adds two further layers that a visitor must read together. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity (June 2025) records a Kaduna secular Penal Code adopted in 2017 whose Section 259 punishes 'unnatural offences' (sodomy, lesbianism and bestiality) with up to 21 years' imprisonment and a fine. Running in parallel is the Kaduna Sharia Penal Code Law 2002 (Law No. 4 of 2002), which applies to Muslims.

The Sharia layer is Kaduna's own promulgated code, not a federal instrument. Ostien's annotated compilation of northern Sharia legislation gives the Sharia Penal Code Law 2002 as Law No. 4 of 2002, signed and brought into operation on 21 June 2002, published in Kaduna State Gazette No. 17 Vol. 36 of 4 July 2002 at pp. A15-A108, and bound together with the Sharia Criminal Procedure Code.

The enacted text fixes stoning to death as the maximum for liwat, or sodomy. Ostien's annotation records Kaduna as one of only three states whose text reads 'Whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm)', with no graduation between unmarried and married offenders, while the lesbianism offence is left to ta'azir, the qadi's discretionary punishment. The UK Home Office note carries the same penalty for Kaduna in its twelve-state table: death by stoning as the maximum for liwat, and same-sex acts between women punishable at the discretion of the qadi (Sharia court judge).

Kaduna is among the twelve states in which Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases, the only states where they do, an arrangement in place since 2002. Sharia criminal proceedings in Kaduna therefore run under the procedure bound with the 2002 code.

Personal scope separates the two Kaduna layers. The 2002 Sharia code applies to Muslims; the 2017 secular code applies across the state irrespective of religion. A visitor's exposure turns on which system handles the matter. Both sets of provisions are drafted around acts rather than identity, with the capital maximum attached to sodomy and a discretionary penalty to acts between women, so a trans visitor's position depends on how their conduct or presentation is classified under the code that is applied.
tangentialFactors:
Kaduna's 2017 secular ceiling of 21 years' imprisonment sits above the federal maximum of 14 years, so a case handled in the state system carries a heavier potential sentence than the national statute provides for.

Within the twelve-state Sharia bloc, Kaduna is one of only three whose enacted text states stoning for sodomy in unconditional terms, without distinguishing unmarried from married offenders. It therefore sits at the bloc's capital ceiling for men's same-sex acts.

The two Kaduna layers also operate through different procedures: the 2002 code is bound with the Sharia Criminal Procedure Code, and cases under it are tried in Sharia courts, whose criminal jurisdiction exists only in those twelve states.
localsOnly:
For residents, the 2002 Sharia code applies personally to Muslims, so a Muslim resident of Kaduna is exposed to its penalties in addition to the state's secular code. The stoning maximum in the enacted text attaches to sodomy, while the lesbianism offence is left to the qadi's discretion rather than a fixed term.

The 2017 Penal Code's Section 259 covers conduct within Kaduna regardless of the person's religion or origin, so residents are charged under the same secular provision as anyone else present in the state, with a maximum of 21 years' imprisonment and a fine.

Kaduna's Sharia courts can try criminal cases, so residents' matters under the 2002 code may be heard in that system rather than in the state's secular courts.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no Kaduna-specific record of arrests, prosecutions, convictions or sentences under either code. Whether the stoning maximum has ever been imposed in the state is not sourced.

The inventory does not establish how the Sharia code's personal application to Muslims is determined for a non-Muslim visitor, nor which code takes precedence where conduct could be charged under both.

Whether either Kaduna provision has been applied to transgender residents or visitors, and how the Sharia courts would classify a trans woman under the sodomy or lesbianism offences, is not addressed by the sources.
